reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .416 xwOBA with a 2.69 xERA on the same Statcast card: there is no comparable profile in the sport. As a hitter, the contact quality is overwhelming — 17.1% barrel rate, 93.6 mph average exit velocity, and a 14.8% walk rate that shows he's working counts and taking what pitchers give him, though a 28.6% whiff rate means he can be beaten with swing-and-miss stuff. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball pairing with 27.9% strikeout rate and a barrel rate of just 3.8% against him explains why the xERA sits that low. The projection, .285/.396/.555 with 39 home runs across 685 plate appearances while also taking the ball as a starter, is less a forecast than a description of what happens when this profile stays healthy, which is the only dependency that matters.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-discipline split is the whole argument: a 17.4% walk rate paired with a 28.4% strikeout rate, which looks like a contradiction until you see the 22.0% chase rate sitting underneath it. He earns the walks by not expanding the zone, and the strikeouts come from swings he does take going wrong, not from getting fooled at the plate. When he connects, the .625 xSLG and 22.7% barrel rate suggest a hitter who punishes mistakes at a level that only a handful of big leaguers reach. The projection of 42 home runs with a .395 OBP in 732 plate appearances is the full translation of that Statcast profile, and the one dependency worth naming is whether that strikeout rate drifts further up as pitchers game-plan him more aggressively into his second full season.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six projected home runs from a 22-year-old, and the Statcast profile says believe it: 93.2 mph average exit velocity with a 51.8% hard-hit rate put him among the most dangerous contact makers in the sport. The .372 xwOBA and .505 xSLG aren't being dragged up by luck — a 12.9% walk rate keeps the denominator honest and a 19.0% strikeout rate means he's not burning at-bats to get there. The whole projection hinges on that plate discipline holding; if pitchers eventually find an exploit in his 28.8% chase rate, which is serviceable but not elite, the ceiling compresses. If it holds, this is a legitimate middle-of-the-order corner bat for a long time, OAA sitting at the bottom of the league and all.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sitting at .311, 100th percentile, tells you the contact quality is already pricing in what the .288 projection still treats as upside. Witt's 93.2 mph average exit velocity and 52.7% hard-hit rate are the engine, and the 33.2% chase rate is the one place the profile gives something back, keeping him from being an automatic on-base threat despite the raw power. Pair 24 home runs with 45 projected stolen bases at shortstop and you're describing a player who, if the plate discipline holds where it is rather than drifting, occupies the conversation about the best all-around position players in the sport without needing a leap in any tool. He's a franchise piece, and the Statcast profile says the production ceiling is still ahead of what he's done.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xwOBA (.364) and hard-hit rate (48.6%) say the contact quality is already elite-adjacent, but a 35.5% chase rate keeps this profile from being clean. What saves it is the walk rate: 11.2% is genuinely good, which means he's drawing enough free passes to partially offset the swing decisions, and the .864 OPS projection reflects that uneasy balance. If the chase rate drifts down even modestly over the next year, the .361 OBP and .503 projected slug stop looking like projections and start looking like a floor. Pair that contact profile with 29.5 ft/s sprint speed and 38 projected steals, and you have a 30-32 home run, 30-plus steal candidate who is one plate-discipline step away from being a middle-of-the-order anchor.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.71 and the walk rate at 5.5%, and together they describe a pitcher who earns his results rather than getting bailed out by them. Skenes strikes out 29.5% of batters while posting a contact-quality profile that holds hitters to a .258 xwOBA, which means the damage that does happen is mostly superficial. The projection carries him to 183.5 innings at a 3.32 ERA with 222 strikeouts, a workload that assumes Pittsburgh keeps him healthy and builds his usage through a full season. If the innings hold, he's a true staff ace before most pitchers his age have found their footing.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The raw power is genuinely elite — 94.4 mph average exit velocity ranks at the 99th percentile, and a 15.3% barrel rate backs it up, but the 28.5% whiff rate is the whole negotiation with this profile. The bat-to-ball problem is real enough that the projection (.269/.345/.482, 26 HR, 29 SB) essentially banks on the contact staying where it landed rather than improving. If the strikeouts drift back toward where they've been at their worst, the average and OBP compress fast and you're left with a boom-or-bust masher, not the five-category force the projection describes.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: mid-rotation starter or better with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 72.7 IP.
reports.published_report: A 1.4 ERA over 72.7 innings at Double-A isn't a hot month, it's a full argument. Kade Anderson has walked 10 batters all season, and when that translates to MLB context, his projected BB/9 of 2.1 sits more than a full walk below the league average; the strikeout rate translates to 10.0 K/9 against an MLB average of 8.6. Every skill grade in the profile comes back 80, miss, command, dominance, run prevention, so the question isn't whether the stuff is there but whether a 21-year-old left-hander can hold this shape against better hitters as he climbs. If he does, the ceiling is a mid-rotation starter or better, and the floor is a multi-inning arm who still beats most MLB rosters.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.peak_summary: Projection: impact everyday bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is impact over 232 PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate carries this profile: 18% in-level, which translates to 12.3% against an MLB average of 8.5%, and that gap survives the level discount. Eli Willits is 18 years old, playing shortstop at A+, and the .415 OBP is downstream of genuine plate discipline rather than a hot BABIP. The ISO translates thin at .14 against an MLB mean of .15, so the 12 home runs in 347 PA are doing work that the quality of contact may not yet fully support, and whether the raw power develops into something that plays at the highest level is the one real hinge here. If the approach holds and the game power matures, he's an impact everyday bat; if the power stalls, you're looking at an on-base-first regular who lives at the top of a lineup, which isn't nothing.

reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: The .431 xwOBA is in the 99th percentile, and it sits next to a 19.9% chase rate and 16.5% walk rate that explain exactly how he gets there. Soto doesn't beat you with one skill; he makes contact on elite terms, walks at a rate barely any hitter in the sport matches, and barrels the ball 15.0% of the time. The projection, .284/.412/.553 with 36 home runs, is really just the Statcast profile translated into a counting-stat season, and the only thing keeping it from looking conservative is the sprint speed at 25.9 ft/s, which caps his baserunning upside and limits how much the 15 projected steals can grow. Everything else says frontline MVP candidate.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson
reports.published_report: The expected numbers don't match the reputation. Henderson's xwOBA sits at .308 and his xSLG at .391, both well below what you'd expect from a player Baltimore is counting on as a cornerstone, and the walk rate at 7.7% isn't doing enough to close that gap. The hard contact is genuinely there, a 44.7% Hard-Hit rate with 89.7 mph average exit velocity, but he's chasing 32.4% of pitches outside the zone and the barrel rate at 7.3% suggests the loud contact isn't landing in the right spots consistently enough. The projection, .238/.312/.425 with 28 home runs over 718 plate appearances, reads like a solid-average shortstop rather than a star, and it holds if he tightens zone discipline; if the chase rate stays where it is, that .238 gets harder to sustain and the power output leans on counting stats accumulated through volume rather than damage rate.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The 18.4% walk rate is the highest in baseball, and it's doing real work against a 31.6% strikeout rate that would end most profiles before they started. What saves Kurtz is that the contact he makes is genuinely violent: 93.6 mph average exit velocity and 18.1% barrels put him in elite company on quality of contact, and the .379 xwOBA reflects that the damage is concentrated, not spread thin. The projection of .264/.395/.503 with 32 home runs lives or dies on whether he can keep chasing at just 22.8% as pitchers map his swing-and-miss; if that chase rate climbs, the strikeouts compound and the walks shrink, and a .503 slug turns into a much harder argument. reports.name: Kyle Schwarber
reports.published_report: 19.4% barrel rate. That's the whole argument — when contact lands, it lands devastatingly, and a 93.4 mph average exit velo with 53.1% hard contact backs it up in a way that a single number can't fake across a full season. The cost is a 34.8% strikeout rate that sits at the bottom of the league, and an xBA of .246 that explains why the batting average barely clears the Mendoza line's cousin. If the chase rate ever softens, this is a true middle-of-the-order bat; if it hardens, you're still looking at a productive regular, just one who always leaves something on the table.

reports.name: Bryan Reynolds
reports.published_report: That 14.7% walk rate is the engine. Reynolds pairs that elite zone control, a 23.1% chase rate, with a 90.9 mph average exit velocity and a 47.3% hard-hit rate, producing an xwOBA of .369 that the projected .834 OPS more or less faithfully reflects. The whiff rate at 28.4% is the one thing that keeps him from being a truly elite contact profile, but his chase rate is so good that pitchers rarely get to the whiff in the first place. reports.name: Luis García Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .296, which is about as loud as a contact profile gets, and it's holding up because the chase rate is the real problem hiding in plain sight. García hits the ball hard, makes consistent contact when he swings, and the .511 xSLG translates into genuine over-the-fence power for a second baseman, all of which anchors ValuCast's projection of .280/.316/.518 with 29 home runs. But a 40.5% chase rate, the kind that lands in the bottom handful of the league, is the thing pitchers will keep selling him, and a 4.7% walk rate is the predictable result. If quality arms decide to live off the plate and he keeps biting, the strikeouts stay manageable but the on-base number never grows, and a .316 OBP is already thin for a lineup piece. The profile is a legitimate middle-of-the-order bat at second base as long as the contact holds, and a streaky, pull-heavy masher if the chase rate worsens.

reports.name: Joe Ryan
reports.published_report: The strikeout-to-walk gap is the whole engine here: 28.4% K rate, 5.6% BB rate, and a contact-quality profile that doesn't hold up the way those numbers suggest it should. Ryan's xERA sits at 3.19 and the projection lands almost exactly there, which tells you the results are tracking the underlying process rather than running on luck. The red flag is the hard-hit exposure — 41.8% hard-hit rate with a barrel rate north of 10% means he's living on the edge every time contact is made, and the model is essentially betting that his command stays sharp enough to keep the damage in the gaps. If the walk rate creeps and the barrels start leaving the yard, a 3.16 ERA projection becomes a much uglier number in a hurry.

reports.name: Liam Doyle
reports.peak_summary: Projection: back end starter with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 56 IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is loud — 12.1 K/9 at AA, translating to 9.3 against major-league hitters, which sits above a league average of 8.6, but the walks are eating the profile alive. Thirty-three free passes in 56 innings, translating to 4.6 walks per nine in an MLB context where the baseline is 3.2, leaves a K-BB% that barely reaches league average once you run it through the converter. The skill shape here is a 70-grade miss sitting on top of 30-grade command, and that combination either forces a relief conversion or demands a significant mechanical correction before the ETA window of one to two years closes. If the walks come down, there's a back-end starter; if they don't, what's left is a depth arm who strikes guys out and nothing else.

reports.name: Dylan Cease
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing standing between Cease and an argument for the best starter in the American League. His 36.9% strikeout rate and 35.9% whiff rate sit at the outer edge of what starters do in this league, and hitters are averaging 85.7 mph off him, which is what happens when barrels are almost entirely unavailable. The xERA of 2.84 and xwOBA of .264 are not aspirational — they describe what contact he has actually allowed. But 11.0% walks live in the bottom fifth of the league for starters, and every bad inning he has traces back to it; if the command doesn't tighten, the projection's 2.89 ERA and 1.15 WHIP require a lot of stranded traffic to survive. When it holds, he's a true number-one arm posting 239 strikeouts across 170 innings. When it slips, he's still very good, just noisier than the stuff deserves.

reports.name: Casey Mize

His whiff rate at 28.8% is solid without being a swing-and-miss weapon, and the 93.6 mph fastball explains why the chase rate lags — he's not blowing anyone off the plate, so he wins by keeping the ball out of the barrel rather than out of reach. The whole profile hinges on that contact-management game holding; if hitters start squaring him up more consistently, there's no strikeout upside to absorb the damage. At 139.7 projected innings with a 3.28 ERA, he's a mid-rotation arm coming back from what Detroit had to hope wasn't a career-altering elbow issue, and the Statcast numbers suggest the underlying skills are genuinely there.

reports.name: Brandon Lowe
reports.published_report: Thirty-two projected home runs from a second baseman is the headline, and the Statcast profile makes it credible: a 12.5% barrel rate and 90.9 mph average exit velocity put him in genuinely dangerous company for raw power at the position. The problem is that a 34.4% whiff rate and 34.0% chase rate create a real ceiling on what that power translates to, which is why the xBA sits at .246 even as the xSLG reaches .458. If pitchers keep attacking him away from the zone and he keeps chasing, the strikeout rate stays near 26.6% and the batting average lives in the low .240s, but the damage when he connects stays legitimate enough that 630 PA of .473 SLG is a reasonable destination. The whole profile hinges on that tradeoff holding: power tool that works, contact tool that doesn't, and enough walks to keep him a useful regular rather than a liability.

reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the argument for Lagrange, and the walk rate is the argument against him. Across 63.3 innings at AAA, he's punching out 11.8 per nine while issuing 4.7 walks per nine, and when you translate that to a major-league context the picture sharpens only slightly: a 9.6 K/9 against a 4.2 BB/9, with a K-BB% of 13.9% that's basically at the MLB mean. The miss grades at 65 on the skill shape, command sits at 35, and those two numbers together explain why a move to shorter stints isn't a downgrade so much as a structural fix. If the walks tighten in a multi-inning or setup role, he's a useful major-league arm; if they don't, he's organizational depth.

reports.name: Jacob Miller
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 51.7 IP.
reports.published_report: The K-BB% translation to MLB context tells the real story: 10.3%, well below what a major-league average arm posts at 13.5%. That gap is the whole tension in Jacob Miller's profile. He's suppressing runs reasonably well at AA, a 4.2 ERA over 51.7 innings, but the strikeout rate doesn't travel, translating to 7.6 at the MLB level, and the walk rate follows him up the ladder at 3.9. What works here is the run prevention holding the ERA together while the underlying miss rate grades out at 35; if the contact management softens in a tougher environment, there's not enough strikeout margin to absorb it. The ceiling is a multi-inning or setup role, the floor is organizational depth, and the whole projection hinges on whether the command grades up enough to make that K-BB gap survivable.

reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the one thing that keeps this profile from being clean. Suzuki chases at 23.0%, which is genuine elite zone discipline, and he draws walks at 10.2%, but a 25.7% strikeout rate drags against both of those numbers and lands below the median for qualified hitters. Contact quality sits in the middle of the league, 89.0 mph average exit velocity and 40.6% hard-hit, yet his 9.2% barrel rate edges the contact into something more useful than those surface numbers suggest, and the .328 xwOBA reflects a hitter who gets more out of contact than the raw speed would imply. If the strikeouts stay where they are, he's a .261/.343/.454 everyday player who fits cleanly as a second-division regular; if they climb, the walk rate and barrel shape aren't enough to hold the floor.

reports.name: Ryan O'Hearn
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is resolutely ordinary, except for one thing: O'Hearn gets to 44.9% hard contact without chasing, his 32.2% chase rate well below the league norm, and that combination is what drives a projection of .278/.345/.465 with 24 home runs over 568 plate appearances. The xwOBA (.333) and xSLG (.430) both land in the low-61st and 62nd percentiles respectively, which is exactly what a solid second-division regular looks like, not more, not less. Walk rate at 7.7% is below average, so the on-base value leans entirely on the bat making real contact, and if the hard-hit rate softens, the profile thins fast. A useful first baseman on a rebuilding Pittsburgh club, with a ceiling that's essentially what the projection already says.

reports.name: Bryant Betancourt
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is impact over 268 PA.
reports.published_report: Fifteen home runs in 303 PA at AAA and AA, with a K rate that translates to 19.8% against a major-league average sitting at 22.0 — that's a catcher profile that doesn't usually look like this. The raw line (.252/.321/.483) understates the translation: his MLB-equivalent ISO comes out at .165, above a league average of .150, and he's whiffing at a rate that would be below average in the bigs, which is the part that makes the power worth believing. The whole question is the walk rate, a 9% mark at the minor-league level that squeezes down to 8.3% in translation, barely a tick below average, so the approach grade sits at 50 while hit and power both grade out as plus. The profile works as a low-end everyday regular if the contact and power combination holds at the MLB level, and collapses to a bench piece if pitchers find a lane they can exploit consistently, which is why a 70% probability of reaching regular-or-better by near term, with a catcher's glove underneath it, is still a meaningful bet.

reports.name: Jeremy Peña
reports.published_report: The xBA of .294 sitting at the 96th percentile tells you almost everything: Peña makes contact at a quality that most hitters can't match, and he does it with an exit velocity profile that would look ordinary at any other position. That's the core tension. The barrel rate is 3.7% and the hard-hit rate is 38.9%, so the batted-ball shape doesn't generate power the way the contact quality implies it should, and the xSLG settling in the middle of the pack confirms the ceiling on his slugging side. What saves the profile is the 16.2% strikeout rate and 29.1 ft/s sprint speed, which together give him avenues to value that don't depend on him suddenly squaring the ball harder. The projection's .276 average and .335 on-base land him as a solid everyday shortstop, not a star, and that reads right given a Statcast card built on contact efficiency and speed rather than damage.

reports.name: Tanner Scott
reports.published_report: A 3.5% walk rate from a reliever who already runs a 34.7% strikeout rate is the kind of combination that shouldn't exist, and yet here we are. Scott's chase rate sits at 40.7% and his whiff rate at 35.6%, which means hitters are swinging at the wrong pitches and missing them when they do — the 2.65 xERA is what you get when both things happen at once. The 2544 rpm spin on the fastball explains some of the bat-miss; the barrel rate of 6.8% is the one tick that's merely good rather than elite, and the projection absorbs that with a 2.85 ERA over 64.3 innings. Twenty projected saves for a Dodgers bullpen built on committee usage is probably a ceiling rather than an expectation, but the underlying profile makes the ERA look like a real floor.

reports.name: Troy Melton
reports.published_report: The xERA and xwOBA both land at the 89th percentile, and neither is propped up by strikeouts. Melton's K% sits at 21.7, right around league average, but he walks just 5.8% of batters and keeps barrels down to 5.9%, and that combination is what explains the contact quality numbers more than anything he's doing in the two-strike count. The 96.1 mph fastball is there, the whiff rate isn't, so he's living on location and limiting damage rather than overpowering anyone. reports.name: JJ Bleday
reports.published_report: The gap between his .238 projected average and an .813 OPS tells you almost everything: Bleday's value lives in the walk rate. At 13.7%, well above what most lineup regulars produce, he draws enough free passes to push his OBP to .342 despite the thin batting average, and an xwOBA of .368 at the 89th percentile suggests the underlying contact quality is backing up that production. The xBA of .264 is meaningfully better than what the projection prints in AVG, so some of that gap is bad luck, and the 26 projected home runs land believably against an xSLG of .462. The whole profile hinges on zone discipline: if the 23.2% chase rate creeps up, the average craters without the power to save him, and the fielding grade is a liability that limits how much slack a team can give him. Everyday outfielder if the discipline holds; a .240/.340 bat with corner-only defense is a useful regular, not a surplus one.

reports.published_report: The .953 OPS across AA and A+ is the loudest thing in this profile, and the translation says it carries: a 21-year-old second baseman whose ISO converts to .166 against a major-league average of .150, and whose strikeout rate lands almost exactly at the big-league mean of 22.0%. The bat-to-power combination grades 70 on both tools, and 161 PA is enough to take the shape seriously without treating it as settled truth. Walk rate is the soft spot, a 46th-percentile approach that projects to 9.0% at the big-league level, meaning the profile leans hard on contact quality holding rather than on patience carrying him through a rough patch. If the hit tool stays where it is, he's a low-end everyday regular in one to two years; if the contact fades against better arms, there's a bench bat underneath.

reports.name: Jacob deGrom
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is right there in the contact numbers: a 34.4% whiff rate sitting next to a 44.0% hard-hit rate and an average exit velocity of 90.7 mph. That's a pitcher who misses bats at an elite level but gets hurt when hitters do connect, and the xERA of 3.44 is roughly where the two forces settle. The strikeout rate at 30.4% and a walk rate of just 5.5% mean he's still commanding the zone the way only a handful of starters can, and at 97.2 mph on the fastball there's no diminishment story yet. The honest dependency here is health, a 37-year-old coming off multiple elbow procedures, and the projection calls for meaningful innings — if he stays on the mound, a mid-rotation-to-above-average season is on the table; if he doesn't, nothing else in the profile matters.

reports.name: Mike Trout
reports.published_report: The contact quality is overwhelming and the plate discipline is historic, yet the projection lands at .236/.379/.464, and that gap tells the story. His 18.9% walk rate leads the sport, his 19.8% chase rate is equally untouchable, and the barrel rate of 20.0% sits at the 99th percentile. What he's lost is the ability to turn that underlying quality into batting average, with an xBA of .262 trailing well behind what a .409 xwOBA implies he should be generating at full health across 592 PA. Everything hinges on availability: if he gives you something close to that full workload, the walks and the barrel rate produce a useful offensive player at 34, and the .843 OPS projection reflects a real floor, not a ceiling.

reports.name: Joey Cantillo
reports.published_report:
The 30.0% whiff rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and the 11.4% walk rate muffles it.

Cantillo generates swing-and-miss well above average, and the 87.3 mph average exit velocity tells you hitters who do make contact aren't squaring him up cleanly. The fastball sits 92.0 mph with 1866 rpm spin, and his 29.3% chase rate means he isn't expanding the zone to manufacture weak contact, so the walks aren't incidental. If the command tightens, a 3.75 ERA over 157.6 innings with 163 strikeouts is a real mid-rotation outcome. If it doesn't, he's a bulk-inning arm who runs deep counts, gives back the whiff gains with free passes, and lives on the fringes of a rotation.

reports.published_report: The .192 ISO across AA and A+ is what makes Devin Fitz-Gerald worth watching, but it's also the thing you have to translate carefully. At the MLB level that raw power softens to a .138 ISO equivalent, below the major-league mean, so the 13 home runs in 354 PA aren't a preview of a plus-power bat so much as a signal that there's something real to work with. The strikeout rate translates to 24.3% against a league that runs around 22%, which isn't disqualifying but means the hit tool carries the argument, and right now the .231 average and .263 BABIP don't support the contact profile the ceiling requires. reports.name: Aidan Cremarosa
reports.peak_summary: Projection: multi-inning or setup reliever with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 57 IP.
reports.published_report: The WHIP is 0.80. Cremarosa has issued 10 walks in 57 innings at A-ball, a 1.6 BB/9 that translates to a projected 2.6 at the MLB level, comfortably below the big-league average of 3.2, and that's where the believability of this ERA lives: a 2.70 earned run average backed by elite command is a lot sturdier than one backed by a hot strand rate. Two to three years out, and the command grade, graded 75 and the best tool in the bag, has to hold for any of the ceiling to matter.
